concept.technique_name: Volumes and surface areas of solids, with volume conservation on recasting

examples.problem_statement: Calculate the volume and total surface area of a hemisphere of diameter 5.0 cm

solution.operation: Volume of hemisphere = ½(volume of sphere) = ⅔πr³ = ⅔π(5.0/2)³
solution.description: A hemisphere is half a sphere, so halve the sphere formula four-thirds pi r cubed to get two-thirds pi r cubed, then substitute the radius 2.5 cm, which is half the given diameter of 5.0 cm.
Evaluate two-thirds times pi times 2.5 cubed to turn the formula into a number, giving a volume of 32.7 cubic centimetres.

solution.operation: Total surface area = curved surface area + area of circle = ½(surface area of sphere) + πr²
solution.description: Turn to surface area. The outside of a hemisphere has two parts, the curved half-sphere and the flat circular face it sits on, so the total is half the sphere's surface area plus the area of a circle of the same radius.
Simplify that sum: half of four pi r squared is two pi r squared, and adding the circle's pi r squared gives three pi r squared, into which the radius 2.5 cm is substituted.
Evaluate three times pi times 2.5 squared to obtain the total surface area, 58.9 square centimetres.

examples.problem_statement: A rectangular piece of metal having dimensions 4 cm by 3 cm by 12 cm is melted down and recast into a pyramid having a rectangular base measuring 2.5 cm by 5 cm. Calculate the perpendicular height of the pyramid

solution.operation: Volume of rectangular prism of metal = 4 × 3 × 12 = 144 cm³
solution.description: Find how much metal there is to work with by multiplying the block's three dimensions, 4 cm by 3 cm by 12 cm, giving 144 cubic centimetres. Melting changes the shape but not this amount.

solution.operation: Volume of pyramid = ⅓(area of base)(perpendicular height)
solution.description: Bring in the shape the metal becomes: a pyramid's volume is one-third of its base area times its perpendicular height, and the height is the unknown being sought.

Because no metal is lost in the recasting, set the pyramid's volume equal to the 144 cubic centimetres found in step 1 and substitute the rectangular base 2.5 cm by 5 cm, leaving the height as the only unknown.

solution.operation: i.e. perpendicular height of pyramid = (144 × 3) / (2.5 × 5) = 34.56 cm
solution.description: Rearrange that equation to make the height the subject: multiply 144 by 3 and divide by the base area of 12.5 square centimetres, giving a perpendicular height of 34.56 cm.

examples.problem_statement: A rivet consists of a cylindrical head, of diameter 1 cm and depth 2 mm, and a shaft of diameter 2 mm and length 1.5 cm. Determine the volume of metal in 2000 such rivets

solution.operation: Radius of cylindrical head = ½ cm = 0.5 cm and height of cylindrical head = 2 mm = 0.2 cm.
solution.description: The head diameter is quoted in centimetres but the head depth and the shaft diameter are in millimetres, so convert everything to centimetres before any formula is used: the head has radius 0.5 cm and height 0.2 cm.

solution.operation: Volume of cylindrical head = πr²h = π(0.5)²(0.2) = 0.1571 cm³
solution.description: Treat the head as a short cylinder and apply pi r squared h with r = 0.5 cm and h = 0.2 cm, giving 0.1571 cubic centimetres.

solution.operation: Volume of cylindrical shaft = πr²h = π(0.2/2)²(1.5) = 0.0471 cm³
solution.description: Treat the shaft as a long thin cylinder. Its 2 mm diameter is 0.2 cm, so the radius is 0.1 cm, and with length 1.5 cm the same cylinder formula gives 0.0471 cubic centimetres.
One rivet is head plus shaft, so add the two cylinder volumes to get 0.2042 cubic centimetres of metal per rivet.

solution.operation: Volume of metal in 2000 such rivets = 2000 × 0.2042 = 408.4 cm³
solution.description: Scale the single rivet up to the whole batch by multiplying by 2000, giving 408.4 cubic centimetres of metal.

examples.problem_statement: A block of copper having a mass of 50 kg is drawn out to make 500 m of wire of uniform cross-section. Given that the density of copper is 8.91 g/cm³, calculate (a) the volume of copper, (b) the cross-sectional area of the wire and (c) the diameter of the cross-section of the wire

solution.description: The density is quoted in grams per cubic centimetre, so the mass must be in grams to match. Multiply the 50 kg by 1000 to get 50000 g before any division.
Density is mass divided by volume, so rearrange it to make volume the subject: volume equals mass divided by density. This is the relation that turns the given mass into part (a).
Substitute the 50000 g and the density 8.91 grams per cubic centimetre into the rearranged formula, giving the volume of copper as 5611.67 cubic centimetres, the answer to part (a).
Move to part (b). The volume just found is in cubic centimetres, so the wire's length must be in centimetres too: 500 m becomes 50000 cm.

solution.operation: Calculate cross-sectional area using volume and length
solution.description: A wire of uniform cross-section is effectively a very long cylinder, so its volume is cross-sectional area times length. Rearrange that to make the area the subject: area equals volume divided by length.
Substitute the volume 5611.67 cubic centimetres and the length 50000 cm to get a cross-sectional area of 0.11223 square centimetres, the answer to part (b).
For part (c), use the fact that the cross-section is a circle. Since its area is pi r squared, the radius is the square root of the area divided by pi, and the diameter is twice that.
Substitute the area 0.11223 square centimetres into that expression: the radius comes out as 0.189 cm, so the diameter is 0.378 cm.
Give the diameter in the unit a wire is normally quoted in by multiplying the 0.378 cm by 10, making it 3.78 mm.

common_mistakes: Dividing the 50 kg straight by 8.91 without converting to grams, which makes the volume 1000 times too small
Dividing the volume in cubic centimetres by 500 m instead of by 50000 cm when finding the cross-sectional area
Stopping at the radius 0.189 cm and quoting it as the diameter, or forgetting to convert the final centimetres to millimetres

concept.technique_name: Volume and surface area of a frustum of a cone

examples.problem_statement: Determine the volume of a frustum of a cone if the diameter of the ends are $6.0$ cm and $4.0$ cm and its perpendicular height is $3.6$ cm.

solution.description: Read the measurements the frustum formula will need out of the question: end diameters of 6.0 cm and 4.0 cm and a perpendicular height of 3.6 cm.
The formula is written in terms of radii, not diameters, so halve each end diameter: the larger radius R is 3.0 cm and the smaller radius r is 2.0 cm.

State the volume formula for a frustum of a cone, one-third pi h times the bracket R squared plus R times r plus r squared. It extends the cone formula to a cone whose tip has been cut off parallel to the base.
Substitute the height 3.6 cm and the two radii 3.0 cm and 2.0 cm into that formula, so that only arithmetic remains.
Work out the three terms inside the bracket one at a time: R squared is 9.0, the cross term R times r is 6.0, and r squared is 4.0.
Add those three values to collapse the bracket to the single number 19.0.
Multiply the bracket total 19.0 by the perpendicular height 3.6 to get 68.4, leaving only the one-third and the pi to apply.
Take one-third of 68.4 and keep pi as a factor rather than rounding it, giving the volume as 22.8 pi cubic centimetres.
Check the same arithmetic by a different route: divide the height by 3 first, giving 1.2, then multiply by 19.0 to get 22.8 again, which confirms the previous step.
Finally multiply 22.8 by pi to express the volume as a decimal, about 71.63 cubic centimetres.

examples.problem_statement: Problem 25. Find the total surface area of the frustum of the cone in Problem 24.

solution.description: Surface area needs the slant height, which the question does not give, so first apply Pythagoras' theorem to the right triangle formed by the perpendicular height and the difference between the two radii of the frustum from Problem 24.

Set up Method 1, the subtraction approach: regard the frustum as a complete cone with a smaller cone removed from its tip, so its curved surface is the whole cone's curved surface minus that of the removed cone.
Turn the curved surface into a total surface by adding the two flat circular ends, the 3.0 cm radius base and the 2.0 cm radius top, giving the total surface area of 99.6 square centimetres.
Repeat the calculation by Method 2, substituting straight into the standard frustum surface-area formula, so that the two independent routes act as a check on each other.

concept.technique_name: Scaling of volume and mass between similar shapes

examples.problem_statement: Problem 30. A car has a mass of 1000 kg. A model of the car is made to a scale of 1 to 50. Determine the mass of the model if the car and its model are made of the same material

solution.description: Begin by reading what the scale means physically: every length on the model, and not its mass or volume, is one fiftieth of the corresponding length on the real car.

solution.operation: Relate linear scale to volume scale
solution.description: Volume depends on three linear dimensions at once, so the volume ratio is the linear scale cubed: one over fifty cubed, that is one 125000th of the car's volume.
Bring mass into the chain through density. Mass is density times volume, and because the model is made of the same material as the car the densities are equal, so mass is in the same ratio as volume.
Apply that ratio to the given figure: multiply the car's 1000 kg by 1/125000 to get the model's mass, 0.008 kg.
Restate the answer in a unit suited to its size by multiplying the 0.008 kg by 1000, giving 8 g.

examples.problem_statement: A car has a mass of 1000kg. A model of the car is made to a scale of 1 to 50. Determine the mass of the model if the car and its model are made of the same material

solution.operation: Volume of model / Volume of car = (1/50)^3
solution.description: Write the volume relationship straight down: since every linear dimension of the model is 1/50 of the car's, the ratio of their volumes is that scale factor cubed.

solution.operation: Mass of model / Mass of car = (1/50)^3
solution.description: Convert the volume ratio into a mass ratio. The two objects share a material, so density is constant and cancels, leaving mass in exactly the ratio just written.
Substitute the car's mass of 1000 kg into that ratio and evaluate 1000 divided by 50 cubed to obtain the model's mass.
